title: Falcon Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Falcon wells have a 380-foot median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $25,000-$38,600.
h1: What Falcon, Colorado Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land around Falcon means paying close attention to the well permit record, not just the listing description. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records include 3,563 wells, with 1,926 recorded as constructed. Reported depths and yields give a useful starting point for budgeting, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular parcel.

Falcon sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with permits naming Denver, Arapahoe, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records include nearby areas such as Peyton, Cimarron Hills, and Black Forest, so neighboring wells can help define expectations before you buy.

sections.heading: Falcon well depths vary by aquifer and parcel
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Falcon is 380 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 592 feet, while the deepest record reaches 2,770 feet. Depths are not evenly distributed: 44% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 25% are 600 feet or deeper.

That spread matters when you request a drilling bid. A contractor should not price your lot from the median alone. The aquifer named on the permit, local geology, nearby completed wells, casing and grout requirements, and access for the rig can all change the work. Denver Basin wells make up all of the aquifer-designated records, with 1,107 permits naming Denver and 629 naming Arapahoe.

sections.heading: Most Falcon wells report workable household yields
sections.html:
Among the 1,360 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 79%, fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 16% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well in this dataset falls under 1 gallon per minute, but that does not promise the same result on an untested lot. Yield is only part of the question. Storage in the well, pump sizing, pressure equipment, and household demand affect usable supply. Ask for the original well test and permit documents rather than relying on a seller's description.

sections.heading: Falcon water levels need careful interpretation
sections.html:
The median static water level is 114 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 55 to 236 feet. That range affects pump setting, electrical planning, and the amount of water stored above the pump. It also shows why a nearby well's depth alone does not tell you where water will stand in your well.

The decade series does not establish a simple, steady decline. Reported medians were 40 feet in the 1950s, 106 in the 1980s, 148 in the 1990s, 652 in the 2000s, 105 in the 2010s, and 120 in the 2020s. The large variation may reflect different locations, aquifers, and measurement conditions. Treat it as background, not a site-specific water-level forecast.

sections.heading: Falcon's permit history shows sustained drilling
sections.html:
Falcon has a long and active permit history. Records show 11 permits from the 1950s, 24 from the 1960s, 351 from the 1970s, 629 from the 1980s, 736 from the 1990s, 712 from the 2000s, 258 from the 2010s, and 285 from the 2020s. The newest permit in the records is from 2025.

The use mix is primarily domestic or household at 84%, followed by stock at 14%, irrigation at 6%, and monitoring at 2%. The most active drillers in these records are Kunau Drilling Llc, M & B Drilling Co., and Hamacher Well Works Inc. Their historical presence is useful for comparison, but confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and the exact scope of any bid.

sections.heading: A Falcon well budget starts near the median depth
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 380-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $19,000 to $26,600. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $25,000 to $38,600.

That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. A deeper hole can move the price substantially, and the final proposal may depend on access, casing, grout, water testing, pump capacity, trench length, and site conditions. Have the driller separate drilling, completion, equipment, electrical, and excavation so competing bids describe the same work.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention around Falcon. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 36 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not prove that a particular well is affected, but it is a reason to identify nearby sites, test the water, and review available agency records.

Low yield and dry-hole risk still require parcel-level investigation despite the favorable reported yield distribution. Confirm the proposed well location can meet separation requirements from septic systems and other sources of contamination. For a building site, also verify that the well location, septic area, driveway, and future house footprint fit together before excavation or construction starts.

sections.heading: Use neighboring permits before buying in Falcon
sections.html:
Before making an offer, pull the permits and completion records for nearby wells, especially in the same subdivision or along the same road. Compare depth, aquifer, static water level, yield, and construction details. Peyton, Ellicott, and Black Forest can provide broader context, but the closest comparable wells usually deserve the most weight.

For a new build, make the well plan part of the site plan. Obtain a written drilling estimate, confirm the intended household use under the permit, and budget for the complete system rather than the hole alone. Test existing water, inspect pump equipment, and make the contract contingent on reviewing well and septic records when buying an improved property.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Falcon, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Falcon is 380 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 592 feet. About 44% of reported depths fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 25% are 600 feet or deeper. A nearby completed well and its aquifer designation are better guides for a specific lot than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Falcon?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At Falcon's 380-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $19,000 to $26,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,000 to $38,600. Access, casing, grout, depth, equipment, and site layout can change the final quote.

faq.q: How much water do Falcon wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 79% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 16% produce more than 15. These figures describe tested records, not a guarantee for an untested parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Falcon, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records map 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 11 historic mine features, and 36 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well water and review local environmental records. For a property purchase, request recent laboratory results and the well construction documents.

faq.q: Are Falcon well levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Static water levels were 40 feet below surface in the 1950s, 106 in the 1980s, 148 in the 1990s, 652 in the 2000s, 105 in the 2010s, and 120 in the 2020s. The variation may reflect different wells and conditions, so it is not a forecast for one Falcon property.
